source_quality.text_layer: usable prose; formula glyphs lost to legacy encoding and recovered from the page rasters

task_reconstruction: Set Great Lakes levels and releases so six groups of users are served under a changing climate, improving on the current plan with a network, rule curves and a multi-objective search.

section_map.summary: summary: the problem, the two-layer design, the sensitivity and the verdict
introduction: the basin, the two dams, the difficulty, then the method
six assumptions stated as bare bullets, then the notation table
the five-lake chain and the case for a network
the directed graph, the balance and the net supply
the rule curves, the fifty-gate dam and the supply threshold
the rainfall forecast and the synthetic wind
the tributary, the spring melt and the ice
the genetic search and its result
the 2017 check and the water-use regression
sensitivity to rainfall and to snowmelt
strengths, weaknesses and the claimed transfer
the conclusion addressed to the commission
the memo answering the inquiry about the current plan
seven references and a one-line appendix

contributions.summary: a directed five-lake network with the balance written on the edges
release rules that split on the supply and on the level, each a scaled power of the distance from average
six stakeholder objectives solved together inside a box on level and flow

dependency_graph.carries: the net total supply and the level

assumptions.summary: the inflow to each lake equals the outflow of the lake above it
the lake-and-river model is said to generalize across the whole system
the lake level and the river level below it are taken as roughly equal
the dam release follows a plain mechanical rule
water use stands in, roughly, for population, economy and level
high levels raise channel costs and flood damage

data_and_preprocessing.summary: historical supply 1900-2023: maximum 9042, average 7067, minimum 5717 cubic metres per second
levels 75.37, 74.77 and 74.00 metres; river flows 3553, 2968 and 2176 cubic metres per second
the water-use regression on the four annual mean levels, sourced from the basin commission

models.summary: the network balance: change in storage, net basin supply, runoff rise, and the two reach cases
the rule curves: supply, level, four-week rain, synthetic wind and the tributary
the six objectives and the genetic search inside the box constraint
the four-input regression of basin water use on annual mean levels

verification.summary: the recorded 2017 levels all fall inside the seasonal bands
the regression returns 130,860 million litres for 2017
satisfaction stays above 0.97 as snowmelt increases

results_trace.summary: the search returns a best level for each month, grouped into four seasonal bands
2017 is called satisfactory because every recorded level sits inside its band
the best level is read as more sensitive to rainfall than to snowmelt

writing_logic.summary: the summary walks the three parts in order and closes with a stacked verdict
the flow is split into a free case and a dammed case before either equation
the memo names each fault of the current plan and answers it with one feature

language_observations.summary: the plan is praised three times and then raised: promising, reliable, beneficial, and more importantly sustainable
an assumption is kept and corrected in one breath: we still assume the equality, however the amount has changed
a refinement is conceded before it is made: the slow drift was handled, but short swings cannot be ignored
the close turns from the work to a request: it is our sincere hope that the strategies will be adopted

visualization_observations.summary: figure 5: six nodes in a line, a to f, with c joining b, the whole basin as one directed graph
figure 10: the dam with four of its fifty gates drawn
figure 14: the twelve months banded into seasons with the recorded levels against them
figure 15: satisfaction falling faster and faster as rainfall rises

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: a judge looking for a usable plan gets seasonal bands, a worked year and a letter answering the current plan's faults
the memo is addressed to the body that would actually adopt the plan, which is the reader a judge stands in for

weaknesses.summary: equation (9) adds the outflow, so a larger release raises the lake
the below-normal supply branch divides by the distance to a differently named minimum
the numbered shipping yield does not match the general form it instantiates
the hydropower objective depends on the level alone
the eastward wind sum repeats one compass term on both sides
the tributary rule carries a leading minus and reuses one exponent
the ice-jam formula is never written
the strengths credit the search with neural networks and symbolic reasoning
the weakness list blames a network the paper never builds
the regression is offered as proof with no fit statistic

independent_extensions.summary: the same rule structure offered, once retuned, to city water systems and to wetland water levels

unresolved_questions: why equation (9) adds the outflow to the supply
why the below-normal branch uses a differently named minimum
why the numbered shipping yield disagrees with the general form
why the hydropower objective ignores the flow
why the eastward wind sum repeats one compass term
why the tributary rule carries a leading minus and reuses its exponent
why the ice-jam formula is omitted
why the search is credited with neural networks
why the weakness list names a network never built
why the regression reports no fit statistic
why the six assumptions carry no justification
